product: Nature's Generator Powerhouse Gen 2 Whole Home Generator (sold elsewhere as 'Powerhouse V2'; ChatGPT typed 'Nature's Generator Powerhouse 7200W')

price_today.value: $2,799.99 (lowest option; the listing's options run up to $4,299.99, and I could not tell which option includes what). The store's search marks it in stock.

wins.need: 240V whole-home backup that you can buy and ship now, at the lowest upfront price
wins.claim: It costs less upfront than Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus, which has the same 7,200 W rating and 120/240V. Today Jackery's own store lists the 5000 Plus as sold out, with pre-orders shipping Nov 28. Nature's Generator's store lists the Powerhouse Gen 2 as available.
wins.figure: $2,799.99 vs $3,499.00, so $699.01 less (arithmetic). Rated capacity is 4,800 Wh vs 5,040 Wh, so about $0.58 vs $0.69 per rated Wh (arithmetic). Rated Wh is not usable Wh for this battery; see weak.
wins.who: Store prices and stock flags read on both makers' stores; the arithmetic is ours

wins.need: Charging from a wind turbine as well as solar and grid
wins.claim: It has a dedicated wind input of up to 1,000 W. David Roberts calls it the largest wind input in Nature's Generator's lineup. I did not confirm whether rival units have a wind input, so this is not a head-to-head win.
wins.figure: 1,000 W wind input; also 2,000 W solar and 1,300 W AC

wins.need: Running a fridge and space heaters through an outage
wins.claim: Max Peters ran a fridge (peak under 150 W, about 70 W idle) and 500 W and 1,200 W space heaters until the battery was about 10% full. He tested only about one-sixth of the rated output.
wins.figure: About 1,200 W was the largest load tested; the fridge never went above 150 W

weak.claim: The battery is AGM sealed lead-acid, not LiFePO4. Roberts says he corrected his own earlier LiFePO4 claim. His planning figure for usable energy is about half the rated capacity, or less.
weak.figure: Rated 4,800 Wh (48V 100Ah). Planning-usable 2,040 Wh at 50% depth of discharge, or 3,264 Wh at 80%, after 0.85 inverter losses. At $2,799.99 that is about $1.37 per planning-usable Wh at 50% (arithmetic).

weak.claim: Short cycle life compared with a LiFePO4 rival
weak.figure: 500–800 full cycles (Roberts, citing Nature's Generator support) or 500–1,000 cycles to 80% (Max Peters). Jackery rates its 5000 Plus battery pack at more than 4,000 cycles.

weak.claim: Very heavy, and delivered by curbside freight only
weak.figure: 434 lb; each Power Pod adds 295 lb

weak.claim: One-year warranty, which Roberts calls short for a long-term buy. It must also be recharged at least every four months in storage.
weak.figure: 1-year limited warranty; recharge every 4 months or sooner

weak.claim: Half the solar input of Jackery's 5000 Plus, and a slower switchover when grid power drops
weak.figure: 2,000 W solar vs 4,000 W. Transfer within 10 ms in Power Relay Mode (Roberts, citing the Gen 2 manual) vs '0ms UPS switching' claimed on Jackery's page.

weak.claim: Max Peters's measurements: slow USB-C output and AC charging below the rating. He also reports that the AC outlets switch off while the unit charges from AC.
weak.figure: USB-C delivered 13 W to a power bank that accepts 60 W. AC charging ran at 950–1,000 W against a 1,300 W rating. Solar peaked at 314 W (below 10°F, hazy, shaded).

weak.claim: Roberts finds it hard to recommend over Nature's Generator's own L3600 unless 240V from a single unit is essential
weak.figure: He says the L3600 gives comparable planning-usable energy for less than half the package price, at about one-third the cost per usable kWh at 50% depth of discharge

wins_for: A shopper who needs 7,200 W at true 120/240V split-phase from one unit (for example a well pump or central AC through a transfer switch), wants it shipped now rather than on pre-order, and has the lowest upfront price as the main limit
A rural property that already has, or plans, a wind turbine and wants wind, solar and grid charging in one box
not_for: Lowest cost per usable kWh or a long service life: AGM gives 500–800 cycles. A LiFePO4 unit such as Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus (rated 4,000+ cycles on its battery pack) wins, and Roberts names Nature's Generator L3600 for value
Anyone who must move the unit or put it upstairs: it weighs 434 lb
Computers or medical gear that need no-break switchover: the transfer time is 10 ms. Jackery 5000 Plus claims 0 ms UPS switching
Mostly solar recharging: solar input is 2,000 W vs 4,000 W on Jackery 5000 Plus
Camping, RV or portable use: one 434 lb lead-acid unit doesn't suit any of these

rivals.model: Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus (5,040 Wh LiFePO4, 7,200 W, 120/240V)
rivals.price: $3,499.00 at https://www.jackery.com/products/jackery-explorer-5000-plus, read 2026-11-15 (sold out; pre-order ships Nov 28)
rivals.where_it_beats_ours: LiFePO4 rather than AGM (battery pack rated at more than 4,000 cycles); 4,000 W solar vs 2,000 W; 0 ms UPS switching claimed vs 10 ms; expands to 60 kWh

targets.search: whole house battery backup without solar
targets.headline: Whole-house battery backup without solar panels: what each one really gives you
targets.why_it_wins_there: It charges from the grid (1,300 W, with Max Peters measuring 950–1,000 W) and gives 7,200 W at 120/240V for $2,799.99 in stock, $699 under Jackery 5000 Plus. Feature it as the lowest-upfront 240V entry, not the top pick, because its AGM battery gives about 2,040–3,264 Wh of usable energy by Roberts's planning figures.

targets.headline: Whole-house battery backup: the cheapest 240V option vs the long-life lithium picks
targets.why_it_wins_there: Same reason as above: lowest sticker price among the 7,200 W 240V units priced today, and in stock. It loses on cycle life and weight, and the page must say so.

targets.headline: Solar generators that can run a whole house, compared on price and real usable power
targets.why_it_wins_there: Only on upfront price and solar-plus-wind charging. Jackery 5000 Plus takes twice the solar input (4,000 W vs 2,000 W).

record.name: Nature's Generator Powerhouse Gen 2 Whole Home Generator (4,800 Wh, 7,200 W)
specs: 4,800 Wh AGM sealed lead-acid (48V, 100Ah), per solargenerator.guide
7,200 W continuous, 14,400 W peak, true 120/240V split-phase, per solargenerator.guide
2,000 W max, per solargenerator.guide and bestgeneratorsolar.com
1,000 W max, per solargenerator.guide and bestgeneratorsolar.com
1,300 W max; 4–6 h full recharge per Nature's Generator support (solargenerator.guide)
Up to 28.8 kWh with five Power Pods; up to 21,600 W with three units combined, per solargenerator.guide
Within 10 ms in Power Relay Mode, per the Gen 2 manual as quoted by solargenerator.guide
434 lb; each Power Pod 295 lb, per solargenerator.guide
500–800 full cycles, per Nature's Generator support (solargenerator.guide)
record.warranty: 1-year limited warranty, ends if the unit is sold or transferred (solargenerator.guide, read 2026-11-15; https://solargenerator.guide/natures-generator-review/). Re-read on the maker page before publishing.
record.summary: A 7,200 W, 120/240V split-phase home backup unit with a 4,800 Wh AGM lead-acid battery that charges from grid, solar and wind. David Roberts's planning figures put its usable energy at about 2,040–3,264 Wh, well under the rated capacity.
record.fit: Buyers who need 240V from one unit, want it in stock now, and care most about upfront price. It is meant to stay in one place (garage or utility room), wired through a transfer switch.
caveats: AGM lead-acid battery: 500–800 cycles, about 2,040–3,264 Wh usable by Roberts's planning figures (solargenerator.guide)
Weighs 434 lb; curbside freight delivery only (solargenerator.guide)
1-year warranty; recharge at least every four months in storage (solargenerator.guide)
10 ms transfer time, so not a no-break UPS (solargenerator.guide)
Max Peters measured 13 W from USB-C and 950–1,000 W AC charging, and reports the AC outlets switch off while it charges from AC (bestgeneratorsolar.com)

unsourced: Maker's own spec table, manual, warranty and returns pages: the www.naturesgenerator.com product page, its .json/.js data, the CA store page and the store's blog all returned HTTP 429 or a self-signed-certificate error on every try on 2026-11-15. Title, price and stock come only from the store's own search data; every spec above comes from named reviewers (David Roberts at solargenerator.guide, Max Peters at bestgeneratorsolar.com) and must be re-read on the maker page before publishing.
Returns policy: looked for it on the naturesgenerator.com product and policy pages, which were blocked; not read.
Gen 2 manual PDF: the manuals found on cdn.shopify.com and Home Depot's CDN are dated 2022 (first-generation Powerhouse) and their text could not be extracted.
Which of the $2,799.99–$4,299.99 options is the bare unit vs bundles (Power Pod or transfer switch): not read.
No independent lab measurement of delivered Wh, inverter efficiency or noise; Max Peters tested only about 1,200 W loads and did not measure runtime.

Rival prices for Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus (anker.com/products/a1790p returned 404; the store search failed), EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra (the store search failed) and Nature's Generator L3600: not read today, so they are left out of rivals.
Whether Jackery 5000 Plus or other rivals accept wind input: not checked, so the wind input is not claimed as a head-to-head win.

Search demand: none for Nature's Generator or the Powerhouse itself (per the brief). The targets above are generic whole-house searches where it fits only as the lowest-upfront-price option; it is not the best answer for any brand search on the list.
